content.thinking:
I'm noticing a timing discrepancy: the flag change was recorded at 15:32:22 per P1's log, but errors actually began around 15:27, before that logged change event. I need to reconcile this gap rather than assume the flag flip caused the onset.

There's also conflicting flag evaluation data at 15:27 showing a mix of on/off states before settling fully on by 15:28, and the attempted flag revert apparently didn't stop the ZeroDivisionError in spend_summary.py:47, which suggests the failure may not be cleanly gated by the flag at all. With no prior production changes in the 24 hours before onset and no earlier revision to roll back to, I'm trying to piece together what else could explain the root cause.

I'll settle on true: the chain shows the flag enabling a code path that divides by zero, which counts as the mechanism. For the write-up I need to be careful with numbers, using placeholders for error counts and durations instead of actual digits, and avoiding exposing things like the "spend_summary.py:47" line number since only bracketed names should contain digits.

For action items, I'm thinking through mitigation (fix the division guard), detection (alert on the error signature, canary before rollout), process fixes (verify flag revert timestamps, wait longer before confirming recovery), and prevention (ensure a prior revision is always available to roll back to). I'm also noting a contributing factor: there was no previous revision available to roll back to, and memory showed the flag revert had already failed once before being retried.

AI-4 (detect): gate flag rollout with error-rate monitoring and accurate change timestamps, possibly alerting on the specific error signature.

For lessons learned, I note what went well—Argus reverted the flag and escalated quickly once rollback proved impossible—against what went wrong, namely the incident staying open with the service still unrecovered. Then I'm laying out impact figures: the fraction of traffic affected, the outage duration, and detection lag, before starting the incident chain with users hitting failing account pages at an elevated error rate.

Working through the why-chain, I trace the ZeroDivisionError failures in the spend summary code path back to the monthly-spend flag being toggled on, but note the evidence is messy—no deploy changes preceded onset, yet the flag toggle timestamp comes after the error onset and reverting the flag didn't resolve things within the wait window. I flag this as an unresolved mismatch and stop short of confirming the root cause since there's no evidence showing what specifically caused the division by zero.

action_items.item: Fix the spend summary so it handles a zero divisor without raising, and add a test that covers the zero case with the flag on.
Make sure a previous known-good revision of the shop service is retained and checked before an incident, so a rollback has something to go back to.
Make the responder check memory for a mitigation that failed on a close earlier incident before it picks the first action. Rank that action lower, or require a stated reason to try it again.

Roll out new flags to a small share of traffic first, with an automatic turn-off if the account page error rate or the ZeroDivisionError log signature rises. Also make sure flag change events are recorded with the true time of the change.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers loading account pages got errors. The error rate averaged {errors_while_broken} while broken and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, against {errors_before} before the onset, and the service had not recovered when the incident was closed.

The failing account page requests died with ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code, {G5309.1} occurrences across {G5309.2} minutes from the onset onward. The other error seen was shoppers closing the connection, which is a small and separate signal.

The spend summary path was being executed because the monthly-spend-feature flag was on. Evaluations were mixed between off and on at the onset, then all on from the next minute. The flag was switched on by admin. The record ruled out an earlier deploy or config change: the first read found {T9.2} production changes before the onset, and the later read found only the flag toggles. Two things stop this from being a clean confirmation. The recorded toggle time is later than the onset, and the mitigation that turned the flag off was refuted because the service stayed at the incident's level. The flag is therefore the likeliest trigger but is not proven to be the only one.

The code on that path divides by a value that can be zero. The record does not show which value was zero or why it was zero for these requests, and no code or data was inspected. The evidence stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend summary division had no protection against a zero divisor, and no test or pre-release check for that case was seen in the record.
Rollback was not available as a fallback: the service had no revision before the one it was running, so the rollback failed and the incident was escalated with the service still failing.

Memory held a close earlier incident where reverting the same flag had not led to recovery. The first mitigation attempt still reverted the flag, and the flag was only moved down the list on the second pass. This cost a verification wait with no improvement.

The flag was enabled for traffic with no staged rollout or error-rate watch tied to the flag change that was seen. The recorded toggle time also did not line up with the onset, which made the trigger hard to confirm. The paging rule waits {rule_waits} before firing, which added to the delay between onset and alert.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers using account pages on the shop service got errors for at least {duration}. The failure rate averaged {errors_while_broken} and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, against {errors_before} normally, so {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have. It began around the time a new spend-summary feature was switched on. The automated responder turned the feature off, but errors continued, so it turned it back on. A rollback was then attempted, but the service had no earlier version to go back to. The incident was escalated to people with the service still failing when it was closed.

went_well: Argus put the flag back as it had found it after the revert was refuted, instead of leaving an unhelpful change in place.
After the first action was refuted, the second investigation widened the log and change reads and came up with a different candidate.
Argus escalated to people straight away when the rollback could not be done.
went_wrong: The service was still failing when the incident was closed, and neither the flag revert nor the rollback restored it.
The first mitigation repeated an action that memory showed had not worked on a close earlier incident.
The flag toggle's recorded time did not match the onset, and the first change read found nothing, so the trigger was never confirmed.

input.root_cause: The account page's spend summary code divides by zero, raising ZeroDivisionError, on the path that the monthly-spend-feature flag enables. Every account page request that reached that path failed. The record does not show which value was zero. It also does not show why switching the flag off did not bring recovery within the wait, so the flag's role as sole trigger is not confirmed.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers
